patient.name: Winston Clarke
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then the cardiology ward
patient.complaint: Two days of fluttering palpitations and breathlessness
background: Drinks about 30 units of alcohol a week
Retired bus driver from Brixton; no drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect an ECG or pulse description ('see item resources') and 'Which is the most likely diagnosis/rhythm?': AF vs flutter vs SVT vs VT, the heart blocks, WPW, or a drug cause.

points: Winston, 76: two days of **fluttering** in his chest.
Breathless walking to the bus stop; no chest pain.
Big weekend of drinking at his grandson's wedding.

steps.lead: Palpitations and breathlessness are the classic complaint. Winston's binge, hypertension and age are typical **causes** to look for.

points: Chest clear; no murmur; no ankle oedema.

visual.title: Winston's 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: No P waves, irregularly irregular narrow QRS at about 138 bpm: **atrial fibrillation with fast ventricular response**.

steps.lead: Winston has a **narrow-complex tachyarrhythmia** (>100 bpm). Next: name which narrow rhythm.

steps.q: No P waves, irregularly irregular, narrow QRS at 138. Which rhythm?
steps.r: Irregular + no P waves = **AF**. Flutter and SVT are regular; VT is broad.

steps.lead: These are the signature ECGs. Winston's matches **AF**; keep the others ready for the distractors.
Winston's **alcohol** excess is a classic AF trigger; rheumatic mitral stenosis is the other one to remember.

visual.title: Contrast: complete heart block
visual.caption: P waves march through at their own rate with **no relationship** to the slow QRS complexes.

steps.text: The bradyarrhythmias are the other half of the topic.

steps.lead: Learn the blocks by the PR interval: long (1st), lengthening (**Wenckebach**), constant with drops (**Mobitz II**), unrelated (**complete**).

steps.q: Winston's BP is 132/84 and he has no chest pain or syncope. Is he unstable?
o: Yes: breathlessness on exertion is shock
Yes: HR over 100 is an adverse feature
steps.r: Adverse features are **shock, syncope, heart failure, ischaemia** or chest pain. Winston has none, so drugs, not shocks.

steps.lead: No adverse features today. If Winston dropped to **BP 70/50** or fainted, he would need **synchronised DC cardioversion**.

investigation.exam: Expect the **12-lead ECG** as gold standard, a **24-hour Holter** for intermittent palpitations, and which score (**CHA2DS2-VASc**) guides anticoagulation.

steps.lead: Winston's diagnosis is made on the **12-lead ECG**. Measure the **PR** and **QT** on every trace.

steps.title: Bloods in ED
steps.text: Low potassium and magnesium after drinking; thyroid normal; no infarct.

steps.lead: Bloods hunt the cause (electrolytes, thyroid) and an **echo** looks for **structural** disease such as mitral stenosis.

points: Echo: left atrium mildly dilated; LV function normal.
No mitral stenosis, no significant valve disease.

steps.lead: Winston's AF was captured on the first ECG. If palpitations come and go uncaptured, use a **24-hour Holter**.
Winston scores **4** on CHA2DS2-VASc, well above the male threshold of 1. **ORBIT**: age 75+ gives 1; otherwise low bleeding risk.
These are the numbers to know: **CHA2DS2-VASc** (men ≥1, women ≥2), **ORBIT** for bleeding, and QTc limits for long QT.

steps.text: Do not mix the scores: **CHA2DS2-VASc** decides anticoagulation in AF; ABCD2 is for TIA; ORBIT is bleeding risk.

management.exam: Expect 'next most appropriate step': adverse features → DC cardioversion; otherwise AF rate control, SVT vagal then adenosine, bradycardia atropine, VT amiodarone, torsades magnesium.

steps.title: Tachyarrhythmia: what to do first
nodes: Adverse features? (shock, syncope, heart failure, ischaemia)
Yes → synchronised DC cardioversion, up to 3 shocks
No, narrow regular (SVT) → vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine
steps.caption: Adverse features first; then QRS width and regularity choose the drug.

steps.q: Winston is stable in AF at 138 bpm. He has no asthma. First-line treatment?
steps.r: Stable AF: **rate control** with a beta-blocker. Adenosine is for SVT; shocks for adverse features.

steps.lead: Winston starts **bisoprolol**. With asthma he would get **diltiazem or verapamil** instead.

visual.title: Winston's heart rate on bisoprolol
visual.caption: Rate control, not rhythm: he stays in AF but the ventricles slow.

steps.lead: If bisoprolol had not slowed him, **digoxin** is second-line. The SVT and bradycardia ladders are here too.
With a CHA2DS2-VASc of 4, Winston starts **apixaban**, a DOAC, for life.

points: Day 3: chest infection; a junior prescribes **clarithromycin**.
Day 4: he faints on the ward.
Monitor: runs of broad complexes **twisting** around the baseline.
Runs self-terminate; he wakes, pulse present between runs.

visual.title: Winston's QTc on day 4
visual.label: Winston 532 ms
visual.caption: Macrolide + low K⁺ and Mg²⁺ pushed his QTc past 500.

steps.q: Polymorphic VT twisting around the baseline with QTc 532. Which drug?
steps.r: Torsades de pointes: **IV magnesium sulphate 2 g**, stop the culprit drug, correct potassium.

steps.lead: Winston gets **magnesium sulphate 2 g IV**, clarithromycin is stopped, and potassium is replaced. Learn the other emergency rules here too.
Ablation is not needed for Winston now. **Radiofrequency ablation** is for refractory AF or **WPW**; VT survivors get an **ICD**.

steps.text: Drug pairs: **SVT = vagal + adenosine; AF = rate control; bradycardia = atropine; VT = amiodarone; torsades = magnesium**.
Never give **verapamil** to a broad-complex tachycardia or with a beta-blocker: it can cause complete heart block or arrest.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanisms: re-entry, the bundle of Kent, why AF causes stroke, why QT prolongation causes torsades.

steps.lead: Most tachyarrhythmias are **re-entry** or abnormal **automaticity**. In WPW, the **bundle of Kent** short-circuits the AV node.
Winston's atria fire chaotically, so no P waves form, and the AV node lets impulses through **unpredictably**.

steps.title: Why AF causes strokes
nodes: Blood stagnates in the left atrial appendage

steps.lead: This is why Winston's apixaban matters more than his heart rate: **left atrial appendage** stasis causes clot.
Clarithromycin **delayed repolarisation**, triggering **early afterdepolarisations**. Magnesium stabilises the membrane.
Torsades can degenerate into **VF**: no coordinated contraction and **no cardiac output**.
Heart block is the opposite problem: conduction failing at or below the **AV node**, from slow PR to complete dissociation.

steps.q: Why does AF give an irregularly irregular pulse?
o: An accessory pathway bypasses the AV node
The AV node conducts chaotic atrial impulses unpredictably
The SA node fires faster during inspiration
steps.r: Chaotic atrial activity bombards the **AV node**, which passes impulses through at random intervals.

o: Delta wave, short PR, broad QRS
mcq.r: **Delta wave** (slurred upstroke), PR <120 ms, broad QRS.

mcq.q: Constant PR with intermittently dropped QRS?
mcq.r: Constant PR + drops = **Mobitz II**; lengthening PR = Wenckebach.

mcq.q: Which drug combination classically causes complete heart block?
QTc defining long QT in men?
Recurrent palpitations, normal resting ECG. Next test?
CHA2DS2-VASc threshold for anticoagulation in women?
First-line drug for SVT after vagal manoeuvres fail?

mcq.r: Adverse features → **synchronised DC cardioversion**, up to 3 shocks.
The **bundle of Kent** bypasses the AV node.

technique.stem: A 70 year old woman has had two episodes of dizziness. Her pulse rate is 52 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Her ECG shows a constant PR interval of 180 ms with occasional P waves that are not followed by a QRS complex.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A rhythm diagnosis: read the ECG description, then match it to the block pattern.

clues: not followed by a QRS complex
steps.x: Constant PR plus dropped QRS complexes; symptomatic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Constant PR with intermittent drops: **Mobitz II**.

elim: In complete block P and QRS are unrelated; here conducted beats have a constant PR.
First-degree block has a long PR but no dropped beats.
Wenckebach shows **progressive** PR lengthening before the drop.
Every P would be followed by a QRS.

steps.x: **D. Second-degree heart block (Mobitz II).** Rule: watch the PR. Lengthening = Wenckebach; constant = Mobitz II. Mobitz II risks asystole.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man has had episodes of palpitations lasting 20 minutes, about three times a week, for 2 months. He is well between episodes. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and regular, BP 130/80 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG in clinic shows sinus rhythm.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

steps.x: An investigation question: the resting ECG missed the rhythm, so how do you catch it?
Frequent intermittent symptoms and a normal resting ECG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Capture the arrhythmia: **24-hour Holter**.

elim: Not first to capture the rhythm.
Tests for ischaemia, not intermittent rhythm.

steps.x: **A. 24-hour Holter monitor.** Rule: uncaptured recurrent palpitations = ambulatory ECG.

technique.stem: A 64 year old man has chest pain and breathlessness. His temperature is 36.4°C, pulse rate 34 bpm, BP 85/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. His ECG shows complete atrioventricular dissociation.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate medication to give first?

steps.x: A first-drug question in an unstable patient: identify the rhythm and its adverse features.
Bradycardia with shock (adverse feature) and complete heart block.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Unstable bradycardia: **IV atropine 500 micrograms**, repeat to 3 mg, then pacing.

elim: For SVT; it slows the AV node further.

steps.x: **C. IV atropine 500 micrograms.** Rule: brady + adverse features = atropine first.

technique.stem: A 45 year old woman on citalopram is given clarithromycin for pneumonia. Two days later she collapses. The monitor shows polymorphic broad-complex tachycardia twisting around the isoelectric line. Her QTc is 540 ms.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this arrhythmia?

steps.x: A mechanism question: name the rhythm, then the electrical process behind it.
Two QT-prolonging drugs and torsades.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Long QT = delayed repolarisation → **early afterdepolarisations** → torsades.
**D. Delayed repolarisation causing early afterdepolarisations.** Rule: QT prolongation triggers EADs; magnesium suppresses them.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man has had palpitations and breathlessness for 3 days. He drinks 40 units of alcohol a week. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 132 bpm (irregularly irregular), BP 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. An ECG is recorded (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: An irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia without P waves, in a heavy drinker, is atrial fibrillation.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely diagnosis?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Alcohol, irregular tachycardia, ECG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **AF**: no P waves, irregularly irregular narrow complexes.

elim: Has P waves of varying shape.

steps.x: **A. Atrial fibrillation.** Irregular + no P = AF.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has palpitations that started suddenly while she was running and stopped abruptly 30 minutes later. She felt lightheaded. Her pulse rate during the episode was 186 bpm and regular, BP 112/70 mmHg. Between episodes her ECG is normal with no delta wave.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden onset and termination of regular palpitations with lightheadedness is SVT; no delta wave argues against WPW.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely diagnosis?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Sudden on, sudden off, regular, fast, young.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Gradual onset and offset with exercise.
Rare in a well 27 year old; broad complex.
Needs a delta wave on the resting ECG.

steps.x: **C. Supraventricular tachycardia.** Abrupt onset and termination = SVT.

practice.stem: A 19 year old man has had recurrent episodes of fast palpitations. His resting ECG shows a PR interval of 100 ms and a slurred upstroke to a broad QRS complex. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Short PR (<120 ms), delta wave and broad QRS with paroxysmal SVT is WPW.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely diagnosis?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Short PR, delta wave, broad QRS, paroxysmal tachycardia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Coved ST elevation V1–V2, not a delta wave.
Broad QRS but normal PR and no delta wave.

steps.x: **E. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.** Delta wave = WPW.

practice.stem: A 78 year old woman with hypertension and angina was started on verapamil last week. She already takes bisoprolol. She feels faint. Her pulse rate is 32 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg. An ECG is recorded (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Concurrent bisoprolol and verapamil can cause complete heart block: P waves with no relationship to QRS complexes.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely diagnosis?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Two AV-nodal blockers, profound bradycardia, ECG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Complete heart block**: P waves and QRS unrelated.

elim: Every P conducts; rate would be normal.
Progressive PR lengthening with conducted beats.
Alternating brady and tachy; P waves related to QRS.
Every P is followed by a QRS.

steps.x: **A. Complete heart block.** Bisoprolol + verapamil = CHB.

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis has had palpitations for 2 days. Her pulse rate is 150 bpm and regular, BP 126/78 mmHg. Her ECG shows sawtooth baseline waves at 300 per minute, most obvious in II and V1, with two waves for every QRS.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A regular rate of 150 with sawtooth waves in 2:1 ratio is atrial flutter, often secondary to mitral valve disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely diagnosis?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Valvular disease, regular 150, sawtooth 2:1.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Atrial flutter with 2:1 block**.
**B. Atrial flutter.** Regular 150 = think flutter.

practice.stem: A 56 year old man is treated with clarithromycin for a chest infection. He also takes citalopram. On day 3 he collapses. The monitor shows a polymorphic broad-complex tachycardia whose QRS axis twists around the baseline.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Clarithromycin and citalopram prolong the QT and precipitate torsades: polymorphic VT twisting around the isoelectric line.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely diagnosis?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Two QT-prolonging drugs; polymorphic twisting VT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Torsades de pointes**.

elim: Irregular but not twisting polymorphic complexes.
No clear QRS complexes at all.

steps.x: **D. Torsades de pointes.** Macrolide + SSRI = long QT = torsades.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has intermittent palpitations. He is otherwise well. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and regular, BP 134/80 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: If the arrhythmia is intermittent and not captured on a 12-lead ECG, a 24-hour Holter monitor is next.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate next investigation?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Intermittent symptoms, normal resting ECG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Holter**.
**A. 24-hour Holter monitor.** Catch it on tape.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman is found to be in atrial fibrillation. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. She has never had a stroke or heart failure. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm (irregularly irregular) and BP 142/84 mmHg.
practice.e: Age 65–74 (1) + female (1) + hypertension (1) + diabetes (1) = 4; above the female threshold of 2, so anticoagulate.

steps.x: The lead-in is "What is her CHA2DS2-VASc score?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Age 65–74 (1), female (1), hypertension (1), diabetes (1).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Score **4**: anticoagulate.
**D. 4.** Age ≥75 or stroke would score 2.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has regular palpitations that started suddenly an hour ago. She has no chest pain. Her pulse rate is 190 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. A Valsalva manoeuvre has not terminated it. She does not have asthma.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Stable SVT after failed vagal manoeuvres is treated with IV adenosine 6 mg; DC cardioversion is reserved for adverse features.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the next most appropriate step in management?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Valsalva manoeuvre has not terminated it
steps.x: Stable SVT, vagal failed, no asthma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV adenosine 6 mg**.

elim: For VT or AF with heart failure.

steps.x: **A. IV adenosine 6 mg.** Vagal → adenosine → verapamil.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has palpitations and chest pain. His pulse rate is 170 bpm and regular, BP 72/48 mmHg. He is clammy and drowsy. ECG shows a broad-complex tachycardia with QRS duration 160 ms.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
practice.e: VT with adverse features (shock, chest pain) needs urgent synchronised DC cardioversion; amiodarone is for stable VT.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate immediate management?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
VT with shock: adverse features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Synchronised DC cardioversion**, up to 3 shocks.
**E. Synchronised DC cardioversion.** Unstable = shock.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man is newly diagnosed with atrial fibrillation. He has heart failure and hypertension. His heart rate is controlled on bisoprolol. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. He has no bleeding history.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management to reduce stroke risk?
practice.e: With CHA2DS2-VASc 3 he needs anticoagulation with a DOAC such as apixaban; aspirin is not adequate stroke prevention.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate long-term management to reduce stroke risk?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
CHA2DS2-VASc: CCF 1 + HTN 1 + age 65–74 1 = 3.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **DOAC (apixaban)**.

elim: Antiplatelets do not prevent AF stroke adequately.

steps.x: **A. Apixaban.** Score ≥2 → DOAC.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped her apixaban 2 months ago. She presents with sudden right arm weakness and expressive dysphasia. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm (irregularly irregular) and BP 150/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her stroke?
o: Thrombus from left atrial appendage stasis embolising to the brain
practice.e: In AF the fibrillating left atrium, especially the appendage, allows stasis and thrombus that embolises to the brain.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely mechanism of her stroke?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
AF off anticoagulation, cortical stroke.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Left atrial appendage** thrombus embolised.

elim: Possible in general, but AF off anticoagulation is the key clue.
Gives lacunar strokes, not cortical dysphasia.

steps.x: **E. Thrombus from left atrial appendage stasis embolising to the brain.** Stasis → thrombus → embolus.

prompts.q: How are arrhythmias classified, and what are the narrow and broad-complex tachycardias?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: rate first, then QRS width.

points.p: Tachy >100 bpm, brady <60 bpm
points.why: Bradyarrhythmias are mostly heart block or sick sinus.

points.p: Narrow: SVT, AF, atrial flutter
Broad: VT
points.why: Treat broad as VT until proven otherwise.

prompts.q: Which features tell you AF rather than SVT on history, pulse and ECG?

points.p: AF: irregularly irregular pulse, apical-radial deficit
points.why: Absent A wave on JVP too.

points.p: AF ECG: absent P waves, narrow complexes
points.why: Rheumatic mitral stenosis and alcohol are classic causes.

points.p: SVT: sudden onset and sudden termination, lightheaded

prompts.q: Give the ECG signatures of WPW, atrial flutter, VT, VF and torsades.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one picture per rhythm.

points.p: WPW: delta wave, short PR <120 ms, broad QRS
Flutter: 2:1 sawtooth, V1 and II
VT: ~150 bpm, broad QRS ~160 ms
VF: no clear QRS complexes
points.why: Most common cause of cardiac death.

points.p: Torsades: polymorphic VT twisting round baseline

prompts.q: Describe the ECG of each degree of heart block, and the bundle branch blocks.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: follow the PR interval.

points.p: First-degree: prolonged PR
Mobitz I: PR lengthens until a QRS drops
Mobitz II: constant PR, intermittent dropped QRS
Complete: no P–QRS relationship, cannon A waves
LBBB: broad QRS, WiLLiaM; RBBB: RSR' V1, MaRRoW

prompts.q: What are the adverse features, and which drugs prolong the QT?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: adverse features change everything.

points.p: Shock, syncope, heart failure, chest pain, ischaemia
Asystole risk: CHB broad QRS, Mobitz II, recent asystole, pause >3 s
QT prolongers: macrolides (clarithromycin), SSRIs (citalopram)

prompts.q: Which investigations confirm an arrhythmia and find its cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ECG, bloods, echo, then Holter.

points.p: 12-lead ECG: gold standard
Bloods (electrolytes) and echocardiogram
24-hour Holter if recurrent and uncaptured
points.why: Normal resting ECG does not exclude it.

prompts.q: What makes up CHA2DS2-VASc, what are the thresholds, and what does ORBIT measure?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: count the points, compare by sex.

points.p: 1 each: CCF, hypertension, age 65–74, diabetes, vascular disease, female
2 each: age ≥75, prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism
Anticoagulate men ≥1, women ≥2
ORBIT: bleeding risk (age 75+, anaemia, bleeding, eGFR <60)

prompts.q: Give the first-line and second-line treatment for AF, SVT and bradycardia.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one ladder per rhythm.

points.p: AF: bisoprolol or diltiazem/verapamil; then digoxin
SVT: vagal manoeuvres, then IV adenosine 6 mg
Bradycardia: IV atropine 500 micrograms, up to 3 mg
Beta-blocker overdose bradycardia: glucagon

prompts.q: How do you manage unstable tachyarrhythmia, stable VT and torsades in an emergency?

points.p: Adverse features: synchronised DC cardioversion, up to 3 shocks
Stable VT: amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min, then 900 mg over 24 h
Torsades: IV magnesium sulphate 2 g

prompts.q: What is the long-term and definitive management of AF, WPW, VT and complete heart block?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: device or ablation for each.

points.p: AF: DOAC (apixaban) if CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2; ablation if refractory
WPW: radiofrequency ablation of the accessory pathway
VT: ICD; no driving 6 months
Unstable complete heart block: permanent pacemaker

prompts.q: What causes tachyarrhythmias, and why does WPW give a delta wave?

points.p: Abnormal automaticity or re-entry circuits
WPW: bundle of Kent bypasses the AV node
points.why: Early ventricular activation = delta wave, short PR.

prompts.q: Why does AF cause stroke, and why does long QT cause torsades?

points.p: Stasis in the left atrial appendage forms thrombus that embolises
Delayed repolarisation triggers early afterdepolarisations

glossary.Tachyarrhythmia: An abnormal heart rhythm with a rate above 100 bpm.
glossary.Bradyarrhythmia: An abnormal heart rhythm with a rate below 60 bpm.
glossary.AF: Atrial fibrillation: chaotic atrial activity giving an irregularly irregular pulse.
glossary.SVT: Supraventricular tachycardia: a fast, regular, narrow-complex rhythm from above the ventricles.
glossary.AVNRT: AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia; the commonest type of SVT.
glossary.VT: Ventricular tachycardia: a fast, broad-complex rhythm from the ventricles.
glossary.VF: Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic ventricular activity with no cardiac output.
glossary.Atrial flutter: A regular atrial re-entry rhythm with sawtooth waves, often 2:1 conduction.
glossary.WPW: Wolff-Parkinson-White: an accessory pathway causing delta waves and re-entrant tachycardias.
glossary.Delta wave: A slurred upstroke of the QRS from early ventricular activation via an accessory pathway.
glossary.Bundle of Kent: The accessory pathway in WPW linking atria and ventricles, bypassing the AV node.
glossary.Torsades de pointes: Polymorphic VT twisting around the baseline, triggered by a long QT.
glossary.QTc: QT interval corrected for heart rate.
glossary.Long QT: QTc above 440 ms in men or 460 ms in women; risks torsades.
glossary.PR interval: Time from start of P wave to start of QRS.
glossary.Wenckebach: Mobitz I block: PR lengthens until a beat is dropped.
glossary.Mobitz II: Second-degree block with constant PR and intermittent dropped QRS; risk of asystole.
glossary.Complete heart block: Third-degree block: atria and ventricles beat independently.
glossary.Cannon A waves: Large JVP waves when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve.
glossary.LBBB: Left bundle branch block: broad QRS, dominant S in V1, M-shaped R in I/aVL.
glossary.RBBB: Right bundle branch block: RSR' in V1–3 and slurred S in lateral leads.
glossary.Apical-radial deficit: Apex rate exceeds radial pulse because some beats are too weak to reach the wrist.
glossary.Irregularly irregular: No pattern to the beat intervals at all; typical of AF.
glossary.Adverse features: Shock, syncope, heart failure or ischaemia, which mandate urgent cardioversion.
glossary.Synchronised DC cardioversion: An electric shock timed to the R wave to restore normal rhythm.
glossary.Vagal manoeuvres: Valsalva or carotid sinus massage, which slow AV node conduction.
glossary.Valsalva: Forced expiration against a closed airway to increase vagal tone.
glossary.Adenosine: IV drug that briefly blocks the AV node; terminates most SVTs.
glossary.Atropine: Antimuscarinic drug that speeds the heart; first-line for unstable bradycardia.
glossary.Isoprenaline: Beta-agonist infusion used for bradycardia when atropine fails.
glossary.Amiodarone: Class III antiarrhythmic used for stable VT and rhythm control in AF.
glossary.Bisoprolol: Cardioselective beta-blocker used for AF rate control.
glossary.Verapamil: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that slows the AV node.
glossary.Digoxin: Cardiac glycoside used as second-line AF rate control.
glossary.Reverse tick: Downsloping ST depression typical of digoxin effect.
glossary.DOAC: Direct oral anticoagulant, such as apixaban.
glossary.Apixaban: A DOAC (factor Xa inhibitor) used for stroke prevention in AF.
glossary.CHA2DS2-VASc: Score estimating stroke risk in AF to decide anticoagulation.
glossary.ORBIT: Score estimating bleeding risk on anticoagulation.
glossary.Holter: Portable ECG recording over 24 hours or longer.
glossary.ICD: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator; shocks VT or VF automatically.
glossary.Radiofrequency ablation: Catheter heat destroys the tissue causing an arrhythmia.
glossary.Left atrial appendage: A pouch off the left atrium where clots form in AF.
glossary.Early afterdepolarisations: Abnormal depolarisations during repolarisation that trigger torsades.
glossary.Re-entry: An impulse circling a loop of tissue and repeatedly re-exciting it.
glossary.Sick sinus syndrome: Sinus node dysfunction causing bradycardia, pauses or alternating brady-tachy.
glossary.Mitral stenosis: Narrowed mitral valve, usually rheumatic, which enlarges the left atrium and causes AF.
glossary.Glucagon: Hormone used to treat beta-blocker overdose bradycardia by raising cAMP.
